title: Fables and Folktales
objectives: I can tell what a fable and a folktale are.
I can find the moral of a short story.
I can say if a character made a wise or a foolish choice.
I can retell a story with a journey, a trick, or a treasure.
rationale: Fables and folktales use clear characters and one clear lesson, so they are the best place for second graders to talk about choices. The eight words name the kinds of stories (fable, folktale), the lesson (moral), the quality of a choice (wise, foolish), and common story parts (trick, journey, treasure). Children can retell a familiar story with these words, which builds the habit of saying what a story teaches, not only what happens.

passage.title: The Turtle and the Fox
paras: This fable is an old folktale about a turtle. The turtle began a journey to find treasure. A sly fox played a trick on him and said the gold was in the river.
A foolish animal would have jumped in. The wise turtle did not trust the fox, so he checked first and saw only mud. The moral is to think before you act.

qs.q: What does "moral" mean in the story?
qs.why: The moral is the lesson the story teaches: think before you act.

qs.q: Why did the turtle check the river first?
choices: He did not trust the fox.
qs.why: The story says the wise turtle did not trust the fox, so he checked.

qs.q: What did the turtle find in the river?
qs.why: He checked and saw only mud, so the fox told a trick.

teacher.overview: Children learn eight words for talking about traditional stories: the kinds (fable, folktale), the lesson (moral), choices (wise, foolish, trick), and story parts (journey, treasure). Read one fable aloud, then retell with the words. Revisit although, jealous, and promise to explain character choices.

notes.va.fable.n: A fable is short and has a moral; often animals act like people. Use a familiar fable. The Spanish cognate is fábula.
notes.va.moral.n: Ask What did the character learn? then What does the story want us to learn? Children often retell the plot; push toward the lesson. Keep morals to one sentence.
notes.va.folktale.n: Folktales are old stories from a culture, passed along by telling. Use a folktale from a culture your students know. A folktale is not always a fable and may not have a stated moral.
notes.va.wise.adj: Wise is about a good choice, not only being smart. Contrast with foolish using two choices for the same problem. Wisdom and wisely are family words.
notes.va.foolish.adj: Foolish is a mild word for a poor choice; teach it about choices, not about people. Say a foolish choice rather than calling a child foolish.
notes.va.trick.n: Teach the sly-act sense only. A trick in a folktale fools another character; ask whether the trick was kind or unkind.
notes.va.journey.n: A journey is a trip with a start and an end. Map a character's journey with three stops. Children may use trip and journey as the same, which is fine.
notes.va.treasure.n: Treasure means valuable things. Children may think of buried gold only; broaden with the idea that a story can treasure friends, but keep the main sense here.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The fox said the gold was in the river, but the turtle checked first. The turtle did not just believe the fox, so he made a wise choice. The moral is think before you act.'
discuss: Which character in a story you know was wise? What did he or she do?
What trick have you seen in a story? Was it kind?
misconceptions: Children may think the moral is the same as the plot. The moral is the lesson.
Some children think wise and smart are exactly the same. Wise adds good choices.
Children may say a person is foolish; keep the word on choices.
extend: Read two fables and compare their morals.
Have children draw a character's journey as a map with three stops.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit although, jealous, and promise: although the fox was sly the turtle was wise; a jealous character may play a trick; a character may promise to share the treasure.
